outline.section: H2: Why 'Natural' on the Label Doesn't Always Mean Clean
outline.guidance: Explain that the word 'natural' on personal care packaging is not regulated by the FDA for toothpaste — any brand can use it. This section sets up the entire post's credibility. Note that the FDA regulates toothpaste as an OTC drug (when it contains fluoride) or as a cosmetic, but neither classification requires all ingredients to be naturally derived. Briefly mention the pH of toothpaste (should be roughly 6.5–8.5 for oral health) as a formulation quality signal readers can check — this addresses the semantic question 'what is the ph of toothpaste.' Keep this section tight; its job is to earn trust and set stakes, not to lecture.

outline.section: H2: The 7 Ingredients to Avoid in Natural Toothpaste
outline.guidance: This is a brief transitional header only — one or two sentences introducing the list. Something like: 'Here are the seven ingredients worth knowing before your next purchase — what they are, how they function, and why a growing number of people are choosing formulas without them.' Do not list the ingredients here; each gets its own H3 below.

outline.guidance: Explain that SLS is a surfactant (foaming agent) derived from petroleum or palm oil. Its mechanism of harm: it disrupts the oral mucosal epithelium, which can increase susceptibility to aphthous ulcers (canker sores). Cite: Herlofson BB, Barkvoll P (1994) 'Sodium lauryl sulfate and recurrent aphthous ulcers,' Acta Odontologica Scandinavica, 52(5):257–259 — include this citation naturally in prose (e.g., 'A 1994 study in Acta Odontologica Scandinavica found…'). Also note SLS can alter taste perception temporarily by suppressing taste receptor phospholipids, which explains the bitter taste after brushing. Close the sub-section with a 'What to look for instead' callout box note: foaming agents derived from coconut (e.g., sodium cocoyl glutamate) or simply a low-foam formula. Link to the SLS-free toothpaste internal post here.

Explain that artificial sweeteners are added to mask the bitter taste of other ingredients. The concern: while amounts in toothpaste are small and spit out, habitual exposure is questioned for microbiome effects. Note that saccharin in particular has an International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) history (it was previously Group 2B, later delisted, but debate continues). More directly relevant: the oral microbiome can be influenced by sweetener residue. Cite: Suez J et al. (2014) 'Artificial sweeteners induce glucose intolerance by altering the gut microbiota,' Nature, 514:181–186 — note this is gut-focused but relevant to broader microbiome conversations; writer should frame it accurately (oral microbiome parallel, not a direct causation claim). 'What to look for instead' note: xylitol (naturally derived, actually inhibits Streptococcus mutans — briefly note this positive) or stevia.

Triclosan is an antibacterial agent that the FDA banned from over-the-counter antiseptic wash products in 2016, though it had a grace period in toothpaste (Colgate Total used it; it was phased out by 2019 but may still appear in some formulas or older stock). Explain endocrine disruption concerns — triclosan has been shown to interfere with thyroid hormone signaling. Cite: Koeppe ES et al. (2013) 'Relationship between urinary triclosan and parameters of thyroid function,' Thyroid, 23(12):1600–1605. Also note the antimicrobial resistance concern flagged by the FDA. 'What to look for instead': essential oil-based antibacterials like tea tree oil or neem, which have demonstrated antimicrobial activity in oral studies without the endocrine risk profile.

Parabens (methylparaben, propylparaben, butylparaben) are preservatives used to extend shelf life. Concern: they are known xenoestrogens — they weakly mimic estrogen in the body. While research is ongoing, the EU has banned certain long-chain parabens in cosmetics and restricted others. Cite: Routledge EJ et al. (1998) 'Some alkyl hydroxy benzoate preservatives (parabens) are estrogenic,' Toxicology and Applied Pharmacology, 153(1):12–19. Note that parabens appear on EWG's Skin Deep database with moderate concern ratings. 'What to look for instead': natural preservatives such as vitamin E (tocopherol) or rosemary extract.

Propylene glycol is a synthetic alcohol used as a humectant to keep toothpaste from drying out. It is also an industrial antifreeze component, though food/cosmetic grades differ. The EWG flags it as a moderate irritant. Concerns relevant to oral use include absorption through mucous membranes — the oral cavity is highly permeable — and potential systemic accumulation with heavy use. Cite the EWG Skin Deep database rating and note that the FDA classifies it as 'generally recognized as safe' (GRAS) for food use at low levels, but its presence in a daily-use oral product is worth noting for clean-conscious consumers. 'What to look for instead': vegetable glycerin (naturally derived, moisturizing, non-toxic).

Polyethylene microbeads were used in some toothpastes as abrasive scrubbers and for visual texture. The Microbead-Free Waters Act (2015) banned rinse-off cosmetic microbeads in the US, but enforcement timelines varied and international products may still contain them. Beyond environmental harm, dentists flagged that microbeads can lodge in gum tissue, creating pockets for bacterial growth. Cite: Mason SA et al. (2016) 'Microplastic pollution is widely detected in US municipal wastewater treatment plant effluent,' Environmental Pollution, 218:1045–1054 — frame this as environmental evidence of microplastic prevalence. Note the gum tissue concern from dental literature. 'What to look for instead': natural abrasives like baking soda, calcium carbonate, or activated charcoal (used carefully — see note on abrasiveness).

outline.section: H3: 7. Diethanolamine (DEA) and Related Ethanolamines (MEA, TEA)
outline.guidance: DEA, MEA, and TEA are pH adjusters and foam boosters. The concern: they can react with other ingredients (particularly nitrites, which may be present as preservatives or contaminants) to form nitrosamines — compounds classified as probable human carcinogens by the IARC. The EU restricts DEA in cosmetics. Cite: Lijinsky W (1999) 'N-Nitroso compounds in the diet,' Mutation Research, 443(1-2):129–138 — note the nitrosamine formation pathway. Also note the California Prop 65 listing for DEA-related nitrosamines. 'What to look for instead': formulas that use naturally alkaline ingredients like baking soda for pH balance, avoiding the need for ethanolamines entirely.

outline.section: H2: A Note on Fluoride — The Controversial Eighth Ingredient
outline.guidance: Fluoride is conspicuously absent from the numbered list — address this directly and transparently. Acknowledge that fluoride is by far the most debated toothpaste ingredient: mainstream dentistry supports it for cavity prevention; many natural health consumers prefer to avoid it. Present both sides fairly. The 'avoid' case: at high doses fluoride is toxic (briefly note the 'how much toothpaste is poisonous' concern — this is why fluoride toothpaste tubes carry a poison control warning; acute toxicity threshold is approximately 5 mg/kg body weight per the CDC; this is why small children should use only a rice-grain amount). The 'keep' case: decades of clinical evidence support fluoride's role in remineralization. Conclude with: for those choosing fluoride-free, hydroxyapatite is a well-researched natural alternative (cite: Kensche A et al., 2017, 'Efficacy of a mouthrinse based on hydroxyapatite to reduce initial bacterial adherence,' Archives of Oral Biology). Address 'is fluoride in toothpaste necessary' and 'what toothpaste is fluoride free' as in-copy answers. Note that Real Skin Care's natural toothpaste is fluoride-free and formulated with clean alternatives — link to the natural toothpaste collection here.

outline.section: H2: How to Read a Toothpaste Ingredient Label in 60 Seconds
outline.guidance: Give readers a practical, fast-scan checklist framework. Explain that toothpaste regulated as an OTC drug will list 'Active Ingredients' separately from 'Inactive Ingredients' — most of the problematic ingredients appear in the Inactive section, which people often skip. Advise: (1) scan the inactive list for the seven ingredients above, (2) check for any ingredient with 'PEG' or numbered chemical suffixes as a proxy for synthetic processing, (3) look for certifications like USDA Organic or EWG Verified as a shortcut signal. This section makes the post actionable and differentiates it from competitor posts that stop at 'avoid these' without a practical next step. Keep the tone empowering — 'you can do this in under a minute at the store.'

outline.section: H2: What Makes a Natural Toothpaste Actually Natural?
outline.guidance: Pivot to the constructive answer: what should a genuinely clean formula contain? Highlight: baking soda (gentle abrasive, pH-balancing), xylitol (natural sweetener with proven anti-caries effect), peppermint or cinnamon essential oil (natural flavoring with antimicrobial properties), vegetable glycerin (humectant), calcium carbonate (abrasive). This is the section where Real Skin Care's philosophy shines — write from the brand's formulation values, not as a product pitch. Tie in 'what is the best natural toothpaste' as a framing device. Mention cinnamon as a natural flavor option (link to the cinnamon toothpaste collection and the best cinnamon toothpaste blog post). Mention mint as the classic option (link to the mint toothpaste collection).

outline.guidance: Include 4–5 FAQ items targeting semantic search questions. Use FAQ schema. Questions and guidance for each: (1) 'Is toothpaste considered a liquid by TSA?' — Answer: Yes, TSA classifies toothpaste as a gel/paste subject to the 3.4 oz (100ml) liquid rule for carry-on bags. Keep brief; this is a semantic traffic opportunity, not the post's core topic. (2) 'Is natural toothpaste safe for people with braces?' — Answer: Generally yes; avoid highly abrasive formulas; look for low-RDA (Relative Dentin Abrasivity) ratings; fluoride-containing formulas are typically recommended by orthodontists but fluoride-free hydroxyapatite options exist. (3) 'Is toothpaste tested on animals?' — Address cruelty-free toothpaste broadly without naming specific brands; note Leaping Bunny and PETA cruelty-free certifications as signals to look for. (4) 'Can men use natural toothpaste?' — Address the 'is toothpaste made for men' query: toothpaste has no biological gender requirement; 'for men' marketing is largely cosmetic positioning. (5) 'What are the ingredients for elephant toothpaste?' — Briefly clarify this is a chemistry experiment (hydrogen peroxide + yeast + dish soap), entirely unrelated to oral care toothpaste. One or two sentences only; include only to capture the semantic query.
